title: DECam Images RCW 86, Remains of Supernova Witnessed in 185
caption: The supernova remnant RCW 86, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURAT.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), J. Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A ring of glowing debris fills this wide view of RCW 86, in the direction of Circinus. The tattered shell is what remains of a white dwarf star that blew apart more than 1800 years ago, in the first supernova ever recorded.

At the time, Chinese astronomers noted the event as a 'guest star', a new light that suddenly appeared in the sky, and the image's title ties it to the supernova seen in 185. A white dwarf is the dense, burnt-out core of a star, and under certain conditions one can blow itself apart. The blast drives an expanding shell of gas outward, and that shell can go on glowing for many centuries.

The picture covers 45 arcminutes of sky, wide enough to show the whole remnant in a single frame, which is rarely possible. It was captured by the Dark Energy Camera, fabricated by the US Department of Energy, which works on the NSF Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile.

understand.summary: Taken with DECam on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope through broadband g and i filters and a narrow N662 filter. The color mapping isn't published.
